answers.answer: Caching could avoid repeated 80 ms database builds for the popular station-language pairs by returning a reusable copy through a 2 ms cache lookup. Weekly changes make reuse promising, although an acceptable delay after edits still needs to be chosen. Use a key such as station-guide:42:es, including both station ID and requested language so English and Spanish do not share an answer. On a hit, the application finds that key and returns the cached guide without building it in the database; a hit may still be stale. On a miss, the application reads/builds the guide from the database, stores the result under that key in the cache, and returns it. The application performs both the database read and cache fill; the cache does not fetch the guide itself. The database remains authoritative, so losing the cached copy does not lose the guide.

evidence.quote: Keeps a reusable copy of a result. Reading that copy can save database work and shorten the wait for the page.
The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.
The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.
Include the inputs that change the answer. Reusing one person's private result for another person is a data leak.

answers.answer: C receives the old hours. A already fetched them before B committed, and after B deleted the key A repopulated that key with its old result. Deletion removed the entry at that moment but did not prevent a delayed fill from storing stale data afterward. Therefore the team cannot claim every read after B finishes sees the new hours: C is a direct counterexample. A simple way for this endpoint to avoid that stale cached copy is to bypass the cache and read the authoritative database for the hours on every request. With the supplied commit prerequisite, a database read subsequent to B's commit sees the completed update. This costs the database lookup; the lesson does not teach a stronger concurrent-read freshness protocol, and none is needed for the specified sequence.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness. To avoid charging an old price at checkout, validate the price against the authoritative data as part of accepting the order.

answers.answer: Case A: the 12:03 request can use the original cached forecast because its ten-minute TTL has not expired, even though the source changed at 12:02. At 12:11 the original entry has expired, so the request must fetch the source and can store a new copy. Case B: the 12:05 request must fetch the source because memory eviction removed the entry at 12:04, before its TTL ended. The ten-minute TTL limits the lifetime of the entry stored at 12:00 to expiration at 12:10. It does not promise that the cached forecast tracks source changes, that it will remain in memory for all ten minutes, or that the source will be refreshed automatically at 12:10. It also does not bound the age of source data used to fill the entry. Eviction at 12:04 is removal to free memory; expiration is removal or unavailability because the allowed lifetime ended. Both cause a later request to miss.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.
Removes entries to make room. A least-recently-used policy favors removing entries that have not been read recently.
A product can be evicted before its TTL ends. Some configurations reject new entries when full instead of evicting existing ones.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.

answers.answer: Use one shared cache entry for the room map. Today each of the four instances holds an independent copy. Deleting the writer instance's copy leaves copies on the other instances intact; requests routed to those instances can still hit and return the old map. Local reads avoid a network call, but keeping them would require coordinating deletion of all four separate copies to achieve this goal. With one shared entry, every instance checks the same cache service, and one deletion removes the entry that all of them use. Under the stated assumption of no concurrent fills, the next miss reloads the updated database map and can fill the shared cache. The accepted 2 ms network lookup is a cost on each cache read; the shared service also needs operating, and an outage can divert reads to the database. Sharing by itself does not guarantee freshness: the application still needs to perform the deletion.

evidence.quote: Lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. One can hold $20 while another holds $25.
Several API servers use a separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached. They can reuse entries, but each lookup adds a network call and the service needs operating.
Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database.
Remove the cached entry after saving the new price in the database. A later miss reloads it.

answers.answer: When the popular key expires, many arriving requests can miss together and each start a schedule database read. That duplicates the same work and can exceed the safe 500 reads per second. Coalesce requests for the schedule: when one lookup is already in progress, have concurrent readers wait for and reuse that lookup's result instead of starting another database read. The application then fills the cache and returns the shared result, turning a group of duplicate lookups into one. During a full cache outage, normal cache hits disappear, so sending all 10,000 requests per second to the database would overwhelm its 500-read capacity. A concrete response is to enforce an application-wide fallback budget of at most 500 schedule database reads per second, share any in-progress lookup where possible, and return temporary errors for requests that cannot be served within that limit. The cap must cover all instances together, not allow each instance 500. This directly bounds database work rather than merely relocating every request to it. The product also permits returning a last known schedule for up to 60 seconds if a usable copy is available, but this response can rely on permitted errors and does not assume an unreachable cache can supply that copy. The slides teach coalescing and limiting fallback but do not specify an implementation for enforcing a global limit; a full limiter design is not supplied.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.
A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the product rules permit it.
Falling back to the database is a load decision, not a free recovery path.

answers.answer: Do not add this cache now. Each unique result is read exactly once, so a cache filled after that database read has no future reader to benefit from its stored copy. The original read still costs 2 ms, already well within the 100 ms budget, and ten reads per second is well below the stated database capacity. Filling the cache adds a write and memory consumption for entries that will never be reused, plus another copy to manage; it provides no avoided database reads in this workload. Reconsider if the workload changes so the same result IDs are read repeatedly, especially if those repeated reads create meaningful database load or latency. Then measure response time, database load, hit fraction, and misses to determine whether reuse pays for the added work.

evidence.quote: Before a copy exists, the API still does the database lookup. Storing that copy uses memory and adds a cache write.
First identify repeated work that is worth avoiding. A cache adds another copy to manage.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.
Compare response time and database load before and after caching. Track the fraction of lookups that hit, and what happens during misses.
